ImageDescription.value:
Distorted (warped, partially compressed and fragmented) panoramic photograph of the Government Quarter (Norwegian Regjeringskvartalet) in the Akersgata Street, central Oslo, Norway, and the surrounding areas, taken on an autumn day in 2026.

The Government Quarter is a complex of government buildings housing several offices of the Norwegian government, located approximately 300 m northeast of the Parliament Building Stortinget. On 22 July 2011, the Government Quarter was the site of a car bomb attack carried out as part of the terrorist attacks in Norway. Eight people were killed in the bombing and more than 200 were injured. Several government buildings sustained severe damage. The government subsequently decided to redevelop the complex to meet updated requirements for security, office space and environmental performance. The reconstructed Government Quarter was officially reopened on 13 April 2026, with several ministries returning to the area.

The photograph shows, among other things:

  • R5 (Government Building 5), housing ministry offices and other facilities at Akersgata 59.
  • St. Olav's Cathedral, built in 1856, between Ullevålsveien and Akersveien.
  • Trinity Church, consecrated in 1858.
  • Deich, a forthcoming photography museum in the premises of the former Deichman Public Library at Hammersborg.
  • Construction cranes serving the ongoing building works.
  • An excavation site above the Hammersborg Tunnel, with construction site cabins and barriers. The site is being redeveloped to accommodate the new Government Park, which will lie above a lowered tunnel carrying traffic on Ring 1.
  • Johan Nygaardsvolds plass, a public square in the Government Quarter area.
  • The A-block, one of the buildings in the Government Quarter.
  • The High-rise Building (Høyblokken), a landmark Modernist government building designed by Erling Viksjø.
  • The linden avenue, a historic tree-lined avenue in front of the High-rise Building.
  • The 22 July Centre, a national memorial and learning centre commemorating the terrorist attacks of 22 July 2011, which opened at its new location in the reconstructed Government Quarter in 2026.
  • A memorial to the victims of the 22 July 2011 terrorist attacks: a mosaic by Mathias Faldbakken, displayed on a large supporting frame.
  • The old Government Building (G-block), designed by Henrik Bull and completed in 1906, which houses offices for the Ministry of Finance at Akersgata 40.
  • Office buildings and other premises along Akersgata, including Schibsted's newspaper headquarters, housing the editorial offices of Aftenposten and VG.

Photograph of the Government Quarter (Norwegian Regjeringskvartalet) in the Akersgata Street, central Oslo, Norway, and the surrounding areas, taken on an summer day in 2026.

The Government Quarter is a complex of government buildings housing several offices of the Norwegian government, located approximately 300 m northeast of the Parliament Building Stortinget. On 22 July 2011, the Government Quarter was the site of a car bomb attack carried out as part of the terrorist attacks in Norway. Eight people were killed in the bombing and more than 200 were injured. Several government buildings sustained severe damage. The government subsequently decided to redevelop the complex to meet updated requirements for security, office space and environmental performance. The reconstructed Government Quarter was officially reopened on 13 April 2026, with several ministries returning to the area.

The photograph shows, among other things:

  • Deich, a forthcoming photography museum in the premises of the former Deichman Public Library at Hammersborg.
  • Construction cranes serving the ongoing building works.
  • An excavation site above the Hammersborg Tunnel, with construction site cabins and barriers. The site is being redeveloped to accommodate the new Government Park, which will lie above a lowered tunnel carrying traffic on Ring 1.
  • Johan Nygaardsvolds plass, a public square in the Government Quarter area.
  • The A-block, one of the buildings in the Government Quarter.
  • The High-rise Building (Høyblokken), a landmark Modernist government building designed by Erling Viksjø.
  • The linden avenue, a historic tree-lined avenue in front of the High-rise Building.
  • The 22 July Centre, a national memorial and learning centre commemorating the terrorist attacks of 22 July 2011, which opened at its new location in the reconstructed Government Quarter in 2026.
  • The old Government Building (G-block), designed by Henrik Bull and completed in 1906, which houses offices for the Ministry of Finance at Akersgata 40.
